newsitem.title: USA: McGraw-Hill says not hurt by UPS strike.
newsitem.headline: McGraw-Hill says not hurt by UPS strike.

text.p: The United Parcel Service of America Inc strike has forced McGraw-Hill Cos Inc's huge schoolbook business to switch to other deliverers, but the stoppage has not hurt business, Chief Financial Officer Robert Bahash said Thursday.
"It's not a significant factor at all," said Bahash. "We're using alternative delivery mechanisms at this point...It's more of a nuisance than anything else."
Bahash said shipments in its professional and educational publishing operations have been delayed several days at most.

The company, which mostly used UPS for shipping college and professional textbooks, has switched to the U.S. Postal Service, Federal Express Corp and DHL Worldwide Express for getting textbooks to college bookstores.
"We're getting product out there," Bahash said. "We're just using other sources."
Bahash said revenues would not be affected. "The bulk of our revenues (in textbooks) comes in July and August," he said. "Even a delay of one to two weeks would not affect us."
Bulk shipments of school textbooks have been delivered via truck from its distribution centers in Columbus, Ohio, and Plano, Texas, near Dallas.
Bahash explained that school textbooks are ordered and shipped months in advance, and orders affected now would be for restocking.
If the strike stretched out into months, "Everybody is going to be affected, and there's going to be a slowdown," Bahash said.

McGraw-Hill is one of the largest educational publishers in the world, and its educational and professional publishing division posted revenues of $1.28 billion in 1996, or 42 percent of total company revenues.
UPS and Teamsters officials met Thursday in an effort to break the deadlock. About 185,000 Teamsters have been on strike since Aug. 4.
